title: California
description: California signed, inscribed and dated 'JOSEPH KLEITSCH / CALIFORNIA / 1930' (lower right) and stamped 'Kleitsch' and inscribed 'Mrs. Kleitsch' (on the reverse) oil on canvas 30 1/4 x 40 1/4 in. framed 35 x 45 in.
provenance: The Estate of Ruth Westphal, Newport Beach, California. | | Literature | Dr. Patricia Trenton, Joseph Kleitsch: A Kaleidoscope of Color, Irvine, 2007, p. 24, illustrated. | | In the 1920s Los Angeles was growing rapidly and towns that used to be separate hamlets, such as Alhambra, Fullerton, Whittier and Montebello were becoming part of one large metropolitan expanse. Laguna Beach by contrast, had a campaign to preserve the serenity of the village and surrounding hills. It was this idyllic character that drew Joseph Kleitsch to Laguna Beach in 1928 following his two-year tour of Europe. The years Kleitsch spent painting in Laguna Beach are marked by street scenes in and around the village and expressionistic brushwork. During this time, he increasingly experimented with a combination of quick impasto in some areas, interspersed with areas of fine detail and Pointillist-like color combinations in others. In the present lot, towering eucalyptus trees frame quaint cottages while pedestrians stroll lazily down the sidewalk. This painting exemplifies Kleitsch at the peak of his artistic wisdom, where it is not enough to simply recreate a landscape, but rather create an entire kaleidoscope of both colors and stylistic techniques. California is both a slice of village life as well as a symbolic tale deriving from a lifetime of rich and varied artistic experience.

title: Indian Encampment
description: Indian Encampment signed and dated 'Farny / 1901' (lower right) oil on board 8 x 14 in. framed 16 1/2 x 22 1/2 in.
provenance: Private collection, Arizona, by family descent. | | Despite being both European born and educated, Henry Farny's subject matter is distinctly American, with his working life coinciding with the end of the Frontier Era. Beginning in 1881, Farny made his first of several trips out West where he was witness to vanishing indigenous culture. He documented each of his journeys with sketches and photography, collecting artifacts and mementos along the way, all of which would remain source material for paintings he completed back home in his Cincinnati studio years later. | | Indian Encampment was painted nearly two decades after that pivotal visit and is imbued with nostalgia for the American West that distinguishes Farny from his contemporaries. Hailing from the same generation as Frederic Remington and Charles Russell, Farny exchanges confrontational scenes of domination over Western territories for peaceful snapshots of everyday life. Here two riders and a mother with child are set against the hazy backdrop of changing seasons with snow melting in the distant mountains and flowers blooming in the foreground. The impressionistic palette of sage greens and pale blues demonstrates his acute sense of the color and beauty of the Western landscape. While the scene may be a romanticized view, it succeeds in capturing Farny's devotion to strong and sympathetic depictions of American Indians.

title: Indian Girl
description: Indian Girl (Lolita) unsigned oil on canvas 18 1/4 x 14 1/4 in. framed 26 1/4 x 22 1/4 in.
provenance: Fenn Galleries, Santa Fe, New Mexico. | George Montgomery, Rancho Mirage, California, acquired from the above, 1977. | Palm Springs Art Museum, bequeathed to the above, 2005. | Sotheby's, New York, 6 October 2021, lot 39. | | Exhibited | Seattle, Washington, Frye Art Museum, George Montgomery, May - June 1978. | Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, National Cowboy Hall of Fame and Western Heritage Center, Fechin Retrospective, 13 September - 17 November 1991. | | We wish to thank Dr. Galina Tuluzakova for her assistance in cataloging this lot. | | Indian Girl (Lolita) is a vibrant example of Nicolai Fechin's portraiture from his Taos period. While Fechin first received academic training in his native Russia under the tutelage of Ilya Repin, a history painter whose work often had literary themes, Fechin's preference for portraiture became readily apparent. Over the twenty-nine years Fechin lived in the New Mexico artist colony, he went on to create a signature style that honored both his Russian roots and his contemporary Western subjects. | | Like most early artists in Taos, Fechin became fascinated by the co-existence of Indian, Spanish, and American cultures. Fechin's Russian training and particular use of a palette knife however, made his work distinctive from other artists practicing in the region at the time. Indian Girl (Portrait of Lolita) utilizes the same energetic 'brushwork' for which he is best known today. Orange and vermillion are layered next to each other to create the impression of folded fabric, with traces of lime green added throughout to intensify the warm citrus hues. Fechin succeeds in finding a harmonious arrangement for all these fragments and patches of color, creating an innate unity for all the impulsively rendered brushstrokes. | | Beyond technique, it is the likeness and spirit of the sitter that makes Fechin's portraits so captivating. The sitter in the present lot was used on at least one other occasion in Lolita, illustrated in Mary Balcomb's monograph on the artist. In both works the sitter has her ebony hair cropped at chin length and stares at the viewer with a side-ways glance. When describing Fechin's time in Taos, Balcomb writes, "The portraits are acutely psychological, compassionate, penetrating studies of character, scrutinizing the soul of man...Each is a highly individualized study, yet possessing a generalization or universal quality which evokes memories and associations that relate to all people everywhere." ¹ | | While Lolita is set outdoors, the present lot has a simple cream-colored background which brings all the attention and focus back to the sitter. Her only accessory is a simple bouquet of daisies, a flower that symbolizes purity and innocence. The inclusion of florals in this portrait may also foreshadow Fechin's transitions to still life in his later post-Taos period when he painted, Calla Lilies, Pansies, Irises and Poppies among others. In Still Life with Daisies, sold at Bonhams Bond Street in 2018, Lolita's daisies appear to have been plucked from her delicate hands and rearranged in a glass pitcher. | | Painted during one of the most prolific periods in Fechin's career, Indian Girl (Portrait of Lolita) is an example of the artist's quintessential style that earned him the status of America's premiere portraitist of the southwest in the early 20th century. | | | ¹ Mary Balcom, Nicolai Fechin, San Cristobal: Fechin Art Reproductions, 1999, pp. 74 and 78.

title: Tracking Trouble
description: Tracking Trouble signed and dated with the artist's device 'Martin Grelle / © 95 CA' (lower right), signed and dated again, and titled (on the stretcher bar) oil on canvas 24 x 48 in. framed 35 1/4 x 59 1/4 in.
provenance: Overland Gallery, Scottsdale, Arizona. | Private collection, Vancouver. | | The present scene is set against the Teewinot Mountains in the Grand Tetons, | a locale that Grelle has captured to great effect over the decades. The peaks — the sixth highest in the Teton Range — magnify the grandeur of the unspoiled landscape and heighten the nobility of his Apsaalooke subjects below. In Tracking Trouble, Grelle displays his mastery of capturing details with historical accuracy and the crisp quality of light in the Tetons. The work dates to Grelle's first year of induction into the Cowboy Artists of America — an honor that he aspired to since his early days of training under fellow CA artists James Boren and Mel Warren. Grelle is currently an emeritus member of the CA, having served as a past President and Board member.
